# Baseline HTTP — Step 1: The message contract

This is Phase 0 from your plan: learn request/response before Express. We are **not** opening `express-backend/` yet. First you understand the wire format every framework wraps.

---

## Why this comes first

Your React shell will eventually call an API. Express (then Hono) only parses and builds **HTTP messages**. If you skip this, every later concept — status codes, CORS, cookies, JSON bodies, error envelopes — feels like magic instead of a small, fixed contract.

MDN puts it plainly: HTTP is a **client-server** protocol. The client always starts; the server answers. Messages are discrete requests and responses, not a continuous stream.

Official docs for this step:
- [Overview of HTTP](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Overview)
- [HTTP messages](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Messages)

---

## The mental model (handwrite this)

```
Client (browser / curl / your React app)
   │
   │  1. open TCP (or TLS) connection
   │  2. send REQUEST message
   │  3. read RESPONSE message
   │  4. reuse or close connection
   ▼
Server (your future Express / Hono app)
```

Three properties that will keep showing up in your backend:

| Property | Meaning | Why it matters for you |
|---|---|---|
| **Simple / readable** | HTTP/1.1 messages are text | You can debug with DevTools Network or `curl -v` |
| **Extensible** | Headers carry new meaning | Auth, CORS, content type, request IDs all live here |
| **Stateless** | One request does not know the previous | Sessions need cookies or tokens; the protocol itself does not remember |

---

## Anatomy of every message

Both requests and responses share the same shape (from the messages guide):

1. **Start line** — what is being asked, or how it turned out  
2. **Headers** — metadata (`Name: value`), one per line  
3. **Blank line** — marks the end of the head  
4. **Optional body** — the payload (JSON, HTML, form data, etc.)

### Request example (handwrite and label each part)

Imagine the frontend creates a task:

```http
POST /api/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
Content-Length: 47

{"title":"Ship health endpoint","status":"todo"}
```

| Piece | In this message | Job |
|---|---|---|
| Method | `POST` | Verb: create / send data |
| Target | `/api/tasks` | Which resource |
| Version | `HTTP/1.1` | Message rules |
| Headers | `Host`, `Content-Type`, … | How to interpret the body and where it is going |
| Blank line | (empty) | Head ends here |
| Body | JSON object | The actual data |

`Host` is required in HTTP/1.1. The path alone is not enough; the server uses `Host` to know which site/app this request is for.

### Response example (handwrite and label)

```http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json
Location: /api/tasks/42
Content-Length: 78

{"id":"42","title":"Ship health endpoint","status":"todo","version":1}
```

| Piece | In this message | Job |
|---|---|---|
| Status code | `201` | Outcome (created) |
| Reason phrase | `Created` | Human hint only; clients should trust the number |
| Headers | `Content-Type`, `Location`, … | How to read the body; where the new resource lives |
| Body | JSON | The created resource |

---

## How this maps to your product later

When you eventually hit `GET /health` or `POST /api/tasks`, Express will turn that raw message into something like `req.method`, `req.path`, `req.headers`, `req.body` — and `res.status(...).json(...)` will rebuild a response message. You are learning the **real** thing those APIs wrap.

---

## Practice (do this by hand now)

> “List my tasks” → successful list of two tasks as JSON.

Use method `GET`, path `/api/tasks`, status `200`. Include at least `Host`, `Accept` on the request and `Content-Type` on the response. Invent two small task objects.

**B. Answer in one sentence each** (write them down):

1. Who initiates the conversation — client or server?  
2. Where does “this is JSON” get declared — start line, header, or body?  
3. Why can the server not rely on “the previous request” to know who the user is?

**C. Optional live check** (terminal):

```bash
curl -v https://example.com/
```

Find the request line, response status line, headers, and where the body starts (after the blank line). You do not need to understand every header yet.

---

## Step 2: Methods And Status Codes

Now that the message shape is clear, the next question is: **what is this request trying to do, and how does the server report the outcome?**

That is the job of:

- the **HTTP method** in the request line
- the **status code** in the response line

Official references:
- [MDN HTTP request methods](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods)
- [MDN HTTP response status codes](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status)

---

## Why methods exist

If every request were just “send some data to `/tasks`”, the server would have to guess your intent. Methods make the intent explicit.

For your backend, think of methods as the difference between these actions:

- “show me tasks”
- “create a task”
- “change part of a task”
- “delete a task”

Same resource family, different intent.

### The core methods you need first

#### `GET`
Used to **read** data.

Example:

```http
GET /api/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
Accept: application/json
```

Why `GET`:
- you want data back
- you are not trying to create or modify anything

Typical response:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

[{"id":"1","title":"Write docs"}]
```

---

#### `POST`
Used to **create** something new or trigger processing.

Example:

```http
POST /api/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
Content-Type: application/json

{"title":"Write docs"}
```

Why `POST`:
- the client is sending new data
- the server will usually create a new resource

Typical response:

```http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json
Location: /api/tasks/1

{"id":"1","title":"Write docs","status":"todo"}
```

---

#### `PATCH`
Used to **partially update** an existing resource.

Example:

```http
PATCH /api/tasks/1 HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
Content-Type: application/json

{"status":"done"}
```

Why `PATCH`:
- you are changing only part of the task
- not replacing the whole task document

Typical response:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":"1","title":"Write docs","status":"done"}
```

---

#### `PUT`
Used to **replace** a resource with a full new representation.

You may not need this early if your app mostly does partial edits. Many APIs choose `PATCH` more often for frontend CRUD.

Example idea:

```http
PUT /api/tasks/1 HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
Content-Type: application/json

{"title":"Write docs","status":"done"}
```

Use `PUT` when the meaning is closer to: “this entire thing should now be exactly this.”

---

#### `DELETE`
Used to remove a resource.

```http
DELETE /api/tasks/1 HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
```

Typical response:

```http
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
```

Why `204`:
- the deletion succeeded
- there is nothing useful to send back in the body

---

## Why status codes exist

The method tells the server what the client wants.

The status code tells the client what happened.

A frontend should not need to inspect English text like `"success"` or `"oops"` to know the outcome. It should be able to reason from the numeric code first.

---

## The status code families

### `2xx` = success
The request was handled successfully.

The main ones you need:

- `200 OK`  
  Standard success, usually for `GET`, `PATCH`, sometimes `POST`

- `201 Created`  
  Use when a new resource was created

- `204 No Content`  
  Success, but no response body is needed

### `4xx` = client-side problem
The request itself is the problem.

This does **not** mean the user is bad. It means the server could not accept what the client sent.

Important ones:

- `400 Bad Request`  
  Malformed or invalid request shape

- `401 Unauthorized`  
  Not authenticated

- `403 Forbidden`  
  Authenticated, but not allowed

- `404 Not Found`  
  Resource does not exist, or you choose not to reveal it

- `409 Conflict`  
  The request conflicts with current state, very useful later for version checks / optimistic concurrency

- `422 Unprocessable Content`  
  The shape is valid HTTP/JSON, but the submitted data fails business validation

### `5xx` = server-side problem
The server failed while trying to process a valid request.

Most important to start with:

- `500 Internal Server Error`

This means: “the server broke, not the client request.”

---

## How to think about them in your app

For the learning backend, these are good first defaults:

- `GET /health` -> `200 OK`
- `GET /api/tasks` -> `200 OK`
- `GET /api/tasks/123` -> `200 OK` or `404 Not Found`
- `POST /api/tasks` -> `201 Created`
- `PATCH /api/tasks/123` -> `200 OK`
- `DELETE /api/tasks/123` -> `204 No Content`
- invalid JSON/body/schema -> `400` or `422`
- missing fake user/session -> `401`
- task belongs to another user -> `403` or sometimes `404`, depending on your policy
- unexpected crash -> `500`

---

## The “why” behind good API choices

A common beginner mistake is making every response `200` and putting the real meaning inside JSON:

```json
{ "success": false, "message": "Task not found" }
```

That works superficially, but it throws away HTTP's built-in semantics.

Better:

- use `404` when not found
- use `401` when not signed in
- use `201` when created
- use `204` when deletion succeeded

Then your frontend, tests, logs, and tools all become simpler and more honest.

---

## A backend example from your task app

### Create a task

Request:

```http
POST /api/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
Content-Type: application/json

{"title":"Learn HTTP"}
```

Good response:

```http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json
Location: /api/tasks/1

{"id":"1","title":"Learn HTTP","status":"todo","version":1}
```

Why:
- `POST` because a new task is being created
- `201` because creation succeeded
- `Location` helps identify the new resource

---

### Invalid create

Request:

```http
POST /api/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
Content-Type: application/json

{"title":""}
```

Good response:

```http
HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content
Content-Type: application/json

{"error":{"code":"VALIDATION_ERROR","message":"Title is required"}}
```

Why:
- the HTTP message is understandable
- but the submitted data fails domain rules

---

### Missing task

Request:

```http
GET /api/tasks/999 HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
Accept: application/json
```

Good response:

```http
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/json

{"error":{"code":"TASK_NOT_FOUND","message":"Task not found"}}
```

Why:
- the path is valid
- the resource is not there

---

## What to handwrite now

Write these two compact tables.

### 1. Methods table

| Method | Meaning | Task app example |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | Read | list tasks |
| `POST` | Create | create task |
| `PATCH` | Partial update | mark task complete |
| `DELETE` | Remove | delete note/task |

### 2. Status table

| Code | Meaning | Task app example |
|---|---|---|
| `200` | Success | fetched task list |
| `201` | Created | task created |
| `204` | Success, no body | task deleted |
| `400` | Bad request | malformed JSON |
| `401` | Not authenticated | no user/session |
| `403` | Not allowed | trying to edit another user's task |
| `404` | Not found | task id does not exist |
| `409` | Conflict | stale version update later |
| `422` | Validation failed | empty title |
| `500` | Server error | unexpected crash |

---

2. If the server **creates** a new task, which status code is the best default?

4. If a user tries to read a task that does not exist, what status code fits best?
5. If deletion works and you do not need to send JSON back, what status code is ideal?

If you want, reply with your five answers and I’ll check them. After that, the next step should be **headers + JSON + Content-Type/Accept**, because that is the last core HTTP piece before we touch Express.

## Answer check

**1. GET** — right. Read operations use `GET`.

**2. 200** — close, but `201 Created` is the better default.

`200` means “it worked.” `201` means “it worked **and a new resource exists now**.”

RFC/MDN treat `201` as the success code for creation. `200` is legal if you really did not create anything new, but for `POST /api/tasks` the contract is: a new task was born, so use `201`. Pair it with `Location` pointing at the new URL.

**3. 422** — right. The HTTP message is fine; the domain data is not. Empty `title` is a validation failure, not a malformed request.

**4. 403** — this is the important mix-up. A missing task is **`404 Not Found`**, not `403`.

| Code | Meaning | Task-app example |
|---|---|---|
| `401` | Who are you? | No session / no fake user |
| `403` | I know who you are, and you may not do this | You try to delete someone else’s task |
| `404` | That resource is not here | `GET /api/tasks/999` does not exist |

`403` is authorization. `404` is existence.

Some APIs return `404` even when the task exists but belongs to another user, so they do not leak that the id is real. That is a privacy choice. It still is not `403` for “id does not exist.”

**5. 204** — right. Success, nothing useful in the body.

Handwrite this one-liner:

> **`2xx` = outcome. `201` = created. `4xx` = whose fault: `401` identity, `403` permission, `404` missing, `422` invalid data.**

# Step 3: Headers, JSON, and Content-Type / Accept

The start line says *what* and *whether it worked*. Headers say *how to interpret the bytes*.

Official docs:
- [Content-Type](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Type)
- [Accept](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Accept)
- [Content negotiation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Content_negotiation)
- [HTTP headers](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers)

---

## Why headers exist

HTTP is extensible. New behavior is added with headers, not by inventing a new protocol.

Without headers, a body is just bytes. The server cannot know if those bytes are JSON, a form, or an audio upload. The client cannot know if the response is JSON or an HTML error page.

MDN: `Content-Type` is a **representation header**. It names the original media type of the payload.

---

## Two headers that must not be confused

### `Content-Type` — “this message’s body is…”

Sent by whoever is **sending a body**.

- Client on `POST`/`PATCH`/`PUT`: “I am sending JSON.”
- Server on a response with a body: “I am returning JSON.”

```http
Content-Type: application/json
```

If a strict server gets a body it does not understand, MDN says it may answer **`415 Unsupported Media Type`**.

### `Accept` — “please send me back…”

Sent by the **client**, even on `GET` (which has no body).

```http
Accept: application/json
```

MDN: the server uses content negotiation, then tells the client what it actually chose via **`Content-Type` on the response**.

| Header | Who sets it | About whose body? | Typical API value |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Accept` | Client | The **response** they want | `application/json` |
| `Content-Type` | Whoever has a body | **This** message’s body | `application/json` |

A `GET` often has `Accept` and **no** `Content-Type`, because there is no request body.

---

## JSON is not magic — it is a media type

JSON is text that follows a grammar. HTTP does not parse JSON by itself. Your server does, **after** reading `Content-Type`.

MDN’s REST example for a successful create:

```http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "message": "New user created",
  "user": { "id": 123 }
}
```

That is the pattern your task API will use.

---

## Full example: create a task (label these on paper)

**Request**

```http
POST /api/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
Accept: application/json
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 27

{"title":"Learn headers"}
```

- `Accept` — client wants JSON **back**
- `Content-Type` — the request body **is** JSON
- `Content-Length` — body size in bytes (HTTP/1.1 often needs this or chunked encoding)
- blank line — head ends
- body — the JSON

**Response**

```http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json
Location: /api/tasks/1
Content-Length: 62

{"id":"1","title":"Learn headers","status":"todo","version":1}
```

- `201` — created (the correction from Q2)
- `Content-Type` — response body is JSON
- `Location` — URL of the new resource (common with `201`)

---

## What goes wrong without these headers

**Wrong: JSON body, no Content-Type**

```http
POST /api/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000

{"title":"Learn headers"}
```

Express `json()` middleware looks at `Content-Type`. If it is missing or not JSON, `req.body` stays empty. You then “validate” nothing and wonder why `title` is undefined.

**Wrong: client expects JSON, server returns HTML**

```http
HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
Content-Type: text/html

<html><body>Error</body></html>
```

`response.json()` in the browser throws. That is why your plan wants a **consistent JSON error envelope** later, always with `Content-Type: application/json`.

**Wrong media type on purpose**

```http
POST /api/tasks HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: text/plain

title=Learn headers
```

A JSON API should reject this with **`415`**, not try to guess.

---

## Other body types you will meet (do not mix them)

| `Content-Type` | Used for | Later in your plan |
|---|---|---|
| `application/json` | Almost all CRUD | Tasks, notes, errors |
| `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` | Classic HTML forms | Not your API default |
| `multipart/form-data` | Files + fields | Dictation audio upload (Phase 5) |

Same `POST`, different body rules. The header is how the server picks a parser.

---

## A few more headers to know, not implement yet

Write the names; we will use them in later steps.

| Header | Role |
|---|---|
| `Host` | Required in HTTP/1.1; which site this request is for |
| `Cookie` | Client sends session (stateless protocol + sessions) |
| `Set-Cookie` | Server starts a session |
| `Origin` / `Access-Control-*` | CORS — next HTTP step after this |
| `X-Request-Id` | Your plan: correlate logs for one request |

---

# Step 4: Origin, cookies, and CORS

HTTP is **stateless**. A `GET` does not remember the previous `POST`. Sessions are bolted on with cookies. Browsers then add a second rule: **scripts from one site must not freely read another site.** That is why your Vite app on one port cannot talk to Express on another until the API **opts in**.

Official docs:
- [Same-origin policy](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Same-origin_policy)
- [CORS](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS)
- [HTTP cookies](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Cookies)

---

## 1. Why HTTP needs cookies

MDN: cookies exist because HTTP has no built-in memory of “this is the same user.”

Login flow in four beats:

1. Client sends credentials (`POST /sign-in`).
2. Server replies with **`Set-Cookie`** containing a session id.
3. Browser stores that cookie and **automatically** sends it later in **`Cookie`**.
4. Server looks up the session and treats the request as that user.

Response (server → browser):

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Set-Cookie: sessionId=abc123; HttpOnly; Path=/

{"ok":true}
```

Later request (browser → server):

```http
GET /api/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
Cookie: sessionId=abc123
Accept: application/json
```

Handwrite:

> **`Set-Cookie` = server plants a note. `Cookie` = browser brings the note back.**

That is how a stateless protocol gets sessions. Your plan’s later Better Auth work is this same idea, with more flags.

`curl` does **not** store cookies unless you tell it to. A browser does. That difference will confuse you if you test only with curl.

---

## 2. Why the browser does not just send cookies everywhere

If `evil.example` could `fetch("https://mail.example/inbox")` and **read the JSON**, it would steal your mail while you are logged in. Cookies would go along for the ride.

MDN same-origin policy: a document from one origin must not freely interact with another.

**Origin** = scheme + host + port.

| URL | Same origin as `http://localhost:5173`? |
|---|---|
| `http://localhost:5173/tasks` | Yes — path does not count |
| `http://localhost:3000/api/tasks` | **No** — different port |
| `https://localhost:5173` | **No** — different scheme |
| `http://127.0.0.1:5173` | **No** — different host string |

Your future layout is exactly that table: Vite on **5173**, API on **3000**. Same machine, **cross-origin**.

MDN also notes: **cross-origin writes** (links, form POST) are often allowed; **cross-origin reads from JavaScript** (`fetch`, `response.json()`) are not, unless CORS says yes.

That is why a form can POST to another site (CSRF risk), but `fetch` cannot *read* the response without CORS. Your JSON API uses `fetch`, so you need CORS.

---

## 3. CORS is the server’s opt-in for browsers

CORS is **not** encryption and **not** authentication. MDN: it is headers that tell **the browser** which other origins may **read** this response.

`curl` and Postman ignore CORS. Only browsers enforce it. If curl works and the React app fails, think CORS first.

### The header pair

Client (browser adds this):

```http
Origin: http://localhost:5173
```

Server must answer something like:

```http
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5173
```

or, for a truly public resource:

```http
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
```

If that header is missing or does not match, JavaScript sees a generic network error. MDN: details are **only in the browser console**, not in `catch` message text.

---

## 4. Two kinds of CORS request

### Simple request

Browser sends the real request immediately. Server still **must** send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` if JS is allowed to read the body.

Example: `GET` with `Accept: application/json`.

```http
GET /api/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
Origin: http://localhost:5173
Accept: application/json
```

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5173
Content-Type: application/json

[]
```

Without `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, the Network tab may show `200`, but **your JS cannot read it**. CORS hides the response from the script, not from the wire.

### Preflight (`OPTIONS`)

If the request is “not simple” — typical for APIs: `Content-Type: application/json`, `PATCH`, custom headers — the browser first asks permission.

MDN: methods that can change data get a preflight: `OPTIONS`, then the real request if allowed.

**Preflight**

```http
OPTIONS /api/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
Origin: http://localhost:5173
Access-Control-Request-Method: POST
Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type
```

**Preflight OK**

```http
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5173
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type
Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400
```

Then the browser sends `POST /api/tasks` with the JSON body.

Your Express app will need to **answer `OPTIONS`**, not only `POST`. That is why CORS middleware exists later. You are learning *why* it exists.

`application/json` is **not** a historical form content type (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `multipart/form-data`, `text/plain`). So JSON APIs almost always preflight.

---

**Short answer:** you learn **authorization ideas early** with a fake user; real **authentication** lands when you port to Hono + Better Auth. Cookies/CORS were the HTTP prep for that.

---

## Authn vs authz (in this course)

| Term | Meaning | When in the path |
|---|---|---|
| **Authentication** | Who are you? (session/cookie/token) | Lightly in HTTP (cookies); **for real in Phase 9 (Hono + Better Auth)** |
| **Authorization** | May *this* user do *this*? | **Phase 1 domain** via fake-user middleware + ownership checks |

---

## Where it sits on the outline

```text
HTTP: cookies + CORS credentials     ← how browsers carry identity
Express shell                        ← done (no real login yet)
Domain CRUD                          ← NEXT: fake user + ownership (authz)
React integration                    ← credentials on fetch; still learning API
SQLite / notes / dictation / agent   ← keep same ownership rules
Hono port                            ← real authn: Better Auth sessions
```

### Phase 1 (Express, soon)
Plan exit criterion: *“prevent cross-user access using a temporary **fake-user** middleware.”*

You will typically:
- Trust a header like `X-User-Id` (or similar) **only in the learning app**
- Attach `req.user` in middleware
- Enforce `task.ownerId === req.user.id` in the **service** (not only in the route)

That teaches **authorization** and consistent `401` / `403` / `404` without building login, password hashing, or session stores yet.

### Phase 2 (React)
`credentials: "include"` and CORS you already set up. The client learns to send cookies when they exist. Full sign-in UI is still not the main Express lesson.

### Phase 9 (Hono port)
This is where **authentication** becomes real:
- Better Auth (already in `backend/`)
- Session cookies, protected routes
- Same domain rules, real identity instead of `X-User-Id`

---

## Why not full auth first?

Real auth mixes many topics (cookies, CSRF/`SameSite`, password/OAuth, session storage, frontend sign-in). The plan isolates:

1. HTTP + API shape  
2. Domain + **who owns what** (fake identity)  
3. Persistence / editor / agent on those contracts  
4. Swap fake identity for Better Auth on the production stack  

So you do not redesign tasks twice around a changing auth system.

---

## One line to remember

> **Authz (ownership) early with a fake user → Authn (login/session) later with Better Auth on Hono.**

When you start tasks, the fake-user middleware is an early milestone inside domain CRUD, not a separate late chapter.
